name: Wendy Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First thing at six I check the shed screens on my phone, temperature, air quality and water, before I've even got my boots on. Then I walk all four sheds, picking up floor eggs, checking for any hens that look poorly, and opening the pop holes so they can go out on the range. Mid-morning is the packing room with our five packers, and in the afternoon I do deliveries to the shops and cafés that take our own-brand eggs. I like the deliveries best, I like a shopkeeper saying our eggs sold out. What wears me out is the bird health side, because I'm still learning it, and when something goes wrong in a shed of eight thousand hens it goes wrong fast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the business and your place in it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's Hillcrest Eggs, thirty-two thousand free-range hens in four sheds, and it's my family's. Mum runs it since Dad had his stroke three years ago, and Dad still does the books from the kitchen table. I came back two years ago from a job in a bank call centre, so I'm the junior, and Mum checks everything I do with the birds. About a third of our eggs go out under our own brand, and the rest go to a big packer on contract.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use it every day. The sheds have sensors, the grading machine has a camera that spots cracked eggs, and I use a chatbot to plan delivery routes and write our posts online. I own a fifth of the business, Mum and Dad gave me shares when I came back, and I've got savings on top. My boyfriend Tom is a police officer, and on Sundays we're both at church with my parents, no excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a bit of a letdown, honestly. I was hoping for more help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth having, and anyone who ignores it is being silly. It catches cracked eggs and writes my posts in five minutes instead of an hour. I'd say that to other farmers and probably online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think these tools are what let a small family business keep up with the big packers. If they stay small and handy, that's still good for us. It just means we keep doing most of it the hard way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy one of the robots that roams the sheds and picks up floor eggs, about twenty thousand, out of my own savings, and pay it back from the extra eggs saved. I'd keep growing our own brand, and push the AI tools further for orders and invoices. No waiting about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit impatient, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you still learning with the birds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spotting trouble early. Mum can walk into a shed and hear that something's off before the screens show anything. The sensors tell me the air's wrong. Mum can tell from the sound the hens make when she opens the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think was behind all the hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tech companies selling, mostly. But I don't blame them, that's their job. I blame people who sit and moan about change instead of getting on with it.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still worth having and anyone who ignores it is being silly, since it catches cracked eggs and writes posts in minutes. I'd say that to other farmers and online.
S0.think: I think these tools let a small family business keep up with the big packers, and that's still good even if they stay small. It just means doing most of it the hard way.
S0.do: Buys a shed robot that picks up floor eggs for about twenty thousand from her own savings and pays it back from eggs saved. Keeps growing the family's own egg brand and pushes AI tools further for orders and invoices.
S0.quote: The sensors tell me the air's wrong. Mum can tell from the sound the hens make when she opens the door.
S0.fieldNote: She's the impatient one, disappointed that the quiet picture offers less help to small businesses. She credits the tools for keeping a family firm competitive and spends her own money on automation readily. Her blame goes to people who complain rather than to companies or government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that sounds like a good one for us, if we're quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for any business willing to work. You don't need a government scheme, you need to get on with it and train your own people. I'd say that at church coffee, which probably makes me unpopular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the packing room changes most. A new packing line could do what our five packers do, faster. But I don't want to put Doreen out of work, she's sixty-one and she packed eggs for my grandad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put in a new automatic packing line within a year, about a hundred and twenty thousand, and use the business savings and a loan. I'd train Doreen and one of the others to run it, rather than let them go. And I'd start delivering local veg and bread alongside our eggs, so the van does more on each run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited. A bit guilty about the packers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Doreen about the new line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you know eggs better than any machine, so you're running it. Doreen taught me to candle eggs when I was six. I'm not going to let a packing line teach her she's not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no government schemes. What about training for people like Doreen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Businesses should do that themselves, like apprenticeships used to be. If I can afford a packing line, I can afford to train Doreen. Too many firms want the machine and none of the duty.

S1.say: I'd say this is good news for any business willing to work. You don't need a government scheme, you need to get on with it and train your own people.
S1.think: I think the packing room changes most, since a new packing line could do what our five packers do. But I don't want to put out of work a sixty-one-year-old packer who worked for my grandfather.
S1.do: Installs an automatic packing line within a year for about a hundred and twenty thousand, using business savings and a loan. Trains two packers to run it and adds local vegetables and bread to her egg deliveries.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, with some guilt about the packers.
S1.quote: Doreen taught me to candle eggs when I was six. I'm not going to let a packing line teach her she's not needed.
S1.fieldNote: She moves straight to buying the machine, but pairs it with a strong sense of duty to an older employee. Her view that businesses, not government, should train people is held with real conviction. The story of being taught to check eggs by that same employee as a child gave it weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's a sprint, and I'm a fast walker, not a sprinter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the businesses that move fast will be the ones still standing. Don't wait for a government plan, because it'll arrive after you've gone bust. I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried that even moving fast isn't enough. If any big company can run robot egg farms at huge scale and write better posts than me with AI, then what's left for us? Just the name on the box and the fact people know my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the sheds and packing as fast as we could get the kit, and put a big chunk of my savings into it. I'd pull back from the packer contract and put everything into our own brand, because that's the part with our name on it. And Tom and I would bring the wedding forward to next summer, because I'd rather be married when everything goes upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be working all hours, which is how I deal with being anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is enough time to buy the robots. It's not enough time to make people care whose eggs they're buying. A brand takes ten years. That's the bit that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom's job, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the other thing. People think police are safe, but if robots can do hands-on work, who knows. I'd pray about that one, honestly, and I'd want him to keep his head down and stay.

S2.say: I'd say the businesses that move fast will be the ones still standing. Don't wait for a government plan, because it will arrive after you've gone bust.
S2.think: I think even moving fast may not be enough if big companies can run huge robot egg farms and market better with AI. We'd be left with only our name on the box and people knowing my mum.
S2.do: Automates the sheds and packing as fast as possible, putting much of her savings in. Pulls back from the packer contract to focus on the family brand, and brings her wedding forward to next summer.
S2.feel: Anxious, and working all hours as a way of coping.
S2.quote: Two years is enough time to buy the robots. It's not enough time to make people care whose eggs they're buying.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture shows her the limit of hustle: she can buy robots in two years but can't build trust in a brand that quickly. Her answer is still to move first and work harder. Worry for her partner's job surfaced here, and she turned to prayer for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Now we're talking. That's enough to build a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it. Build something people trust, and don't wait for anyone to hand you a plan. I'd say it to every young farmer I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd grow. The Morrises down the road have an egg farm and their kids don't want it. If we bought it and ran both with robots under our brand, we'd be big enough to matter and small enough that people still know who we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate our sheds over the first two years, then talk to the Morrises about buying their farm with a loan and my savings in year two or three. I'd spend serious time on the brand, real photos of real hens, of Mum and Dad, of the church fête. And I'd use every AI tool going to run the office side so we stay lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets people get to know us. Anyone can buy a robot. Not everyone can say my dad still does the books at the kitchen table and my mum names the hens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a lot of plans that need loans. What if it goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost money I chose to risk, and I start again. I'd rather fail at something I built than be safe doing something someone else decided for me. Dad says I get that from Gran.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it: build something people trust and don't wait for anyone to hand you a plan. I'd say it to every young farmer I know.
S3.think: I think we'd grow by buying a neighbouring egg farm whose owners' children don't want it and running both with robots under our brand. We'd be big enough to matter but small enough to be known.
S3.do: Automates the family's sheds over two years, then seeks to buy the neighbouring egg farm with a loan and savings in year two or three. Invests time in building the brand and uses AI tools to keep the office lean.
S3.quote: I'd rather fail at something I built than be safe doing something someone else decided for me.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she expands rather than defends, buying a neighbour out and putting her family's story at the centre of the brand. Risk doesn't frighten her; being told what to do does. She rooted that attitude in her grandmother, which fits her strong family identity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to do it properly. And to have children, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for any family business to get ready, so there's no excuse. Train young people, build your name, and stop waiting for someone else. I'd say it at church, at the market, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the farm becomes more of a place people visit than a factory. If robots do the work, people will want to see real hens and real farmers even more. I'd want our children to grow up collecting eggs, even if a robot could do it faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the sheds step by step over five years. Around year three I'd build a small farm shop and a hen walk where families and school groups can come and collect eggs, and I'd take on two local apprentices every year to learn the business. Tom and I would marry and start a family in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Excited, and calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change, compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five, I'm racing to get big. With ten, I can slow down and build the kind of farm I'd want my kids to grow up on, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apprentices, if robots do the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because young people need to learn how to work, whatever the work is. My gran always said idle hands make trouble. I'd rather a teenager learned to handle a hen than sat at home waiting for the robots to pay them.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for any family business to get ready, so there's no excuse: train young people, build your name and stop waiting for someone else.
S4.think: I think the farm becomes a place people visit as much as a business, because with robots doing the work people will want to see real hens and farmers. I'd want my children to grow up collecting eggs.
S4.do: Automates the sheds step by step over five years and builds a farm shop and hen walk for families and schools around year three. Takes on two local apprentices each year and plans to marry and start a family soon.
S4.quote: With ten, I can slow down and build the kind of farm I'd want my kids to grow up on, robots or not.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years let her picture the farm she actually wants, part business and part place for families. Her belief in work as good for young people stayed firm even when robots could do it. Of all the pictures, this was the only one where she sounded relaxed rather than driven.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to build trust in a small brand, and big companies would flood the shops with cheap eggs. And I'd worry about Tom. What would help is fair competition rules so the big firms can't sell below cost to wipe out family farms, and fewer forms so we can move as fast as they can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether people will still want to work. I think they will, I think it's good for us. I'd want somebody making sure there's still a reason to get up at six.

headlineQuote: Anyone can buy a robot. Not everyone can say my dad still does the books at the kitchen table and my mum names the hens.
portrait: Wendy Varga is a 27-year-old junior on her family's free-range egg farm, where she owns a fifth of the business, uses AI tools every day and is still learning bird health from her mother. She is a churchgoer with a police officer boyfriend, believes in self-reliance and businesses training their own people, and blames people who complain rather than act. In AI Plateau and Steady Disruption she quickly buys robots and a packing line, while making sure an older packer keeps her job. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious, because robots can be bought fast but trust in a brand can't. With five years she'd expand by buying a neighbouring farm, and with ten she'd build a family-friendly farm with apprentices and children of her own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to build trust in a small egg brand before big companies flooded the market, and because of the risk to her partner's job.
whatWouldHelp: Fair competition rules that stop big firms selling below cost to wipe out family farms, and less paperwork so small businesses can move fast.
